content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has released updated guidelines for the screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions to prevent cervical cancer. These guidelines emphasize the use of dual-stain cytology as a triage test for women who test positive for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV). Dual-stain cytology detects the presence of two proteins, p16 and Ki-67, which are co-expressed in cells transformed by high-risk HPV. This method is performed on liquid-based cytology (LBC) slides and is not applicable to conventional Pap smears. A positive dual-stain result indicates an increased risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 (CIN 2/3), which are high-grade lesions that may progress to cervical cancer if untreated. Cervical cancer remains the fourth most common cancer among women globally, with approximately 662,000 new cases and 349,000 deaths reported in 2022. It is the most common cancer in women in 25 countries, many of which are in sub-Saharan Africa. However, cervical cancer can be eliminated as a public health problem through the WHO Cervical Cancer Elimination Initiative. This initiative, launched in 2018, aims to achieve by 2030: (1) 90% of girls fully vaccinated with the HPV vaccine by age 15, (2) 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and (3) 90% of women with cervical disease receiving appropriate treatment. The updated guidelines were developed in phases, with the current phase focusing on dual-stain cytology as a triage test. This approach is part of the screen, triage, and treat strategy, where women with a positive HPV test undergo further testing to determine the need for treatment. The guidelines recommend using health worker-collected samples for dual-stain cytology and retesting with HPV nucleic acid tests (NATs) 24 months after a negative dual-stain result. These recommendations are conditional and based on low-certainty evidence. Dual-stain cytology requires specific laboratory infrastructure, including LBC systems and immunostaining equipment, and cannot be implemented as a point-of-care test. It is best suited for centralized, high-standard laboratories serving multiple screening sites. While dual-stain cytology has shown higher reproducibility and faster proficiency in interpretation compared to Pap cytology, its implementation in low-resource settings and validation for self-collected samples remain limited. For women living with HIV, no specific recommendation was made for using dual-stain cytology due to insufficient evidence. The guidelines continue to recommend other triage tests for this population. The WHO guidelines aim to improve national strategies for cervical cancer prevention, including screening and treatment, to achieve the 2030 targets and contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for health and gender equality.
